# 11-issen: sources

Back-test entry `11-issen.yaml`: Issen, an AI voice tutor for speaking a foreign language (YC Fall 2024). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only. Quotes are verbatim. **[author]** marks a choice the public material does not make, kept as small as it could be.

Sources, with the short names used below:
- **HN**: Launch HN, 2025-06-26, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44387828 (the founders' post and 271 comments). A comment is cited as HN/NNN, meaning https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=NNN.
- **YCL**: Launch YC post, https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/MIn-issen-your-personalized-ai-voice-language-tutor
- **YCC**: YC company page, https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/issen

Status today: same idea ("AI realtime voice companion for language learning", YCC).

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (actor, segment).**
- "We started this company after struggling to find great tools to practice speaking Japanese and French" (HN).
- The founders' own line that it is not for beginners, honoured in the segment:
  - "So basically if you are starting a new language from zero, then this is not for you?" "That's correct." (HN/44388670, HN/44388778).
  - "Quite honestly our current focus is more for B1+ students" (HN/44388888).
  - "ISSEN is more focused on intermediate and advanced students, and especially those that are willing to use a more difficult app in order to learn faster" (HN/44391572).
- Segment **[author]**, worded from these: "adults in the US learning a foreign language at intermediate level or above, not starting from zero". One CONSUMER role.
- **[author]** The founders are not US-only. US is the default market and nothing public points elsewhere.

**2. What (the job).**
- "We wanted something that would talk with us — realistically, in full conversations — and actually help us improve" (HN).
- Against streaks: apps where users are "achieving long streaks and so on, without actually getting fluent in the language" (HN).
- Context job **[author]**, worded from these: "become able to hold a real conversation in the language".

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- "Having a tutor can be awesome, but there are downsides: they can be expensive (since you pay by the hour), difficult to schedule, and have a high upfront cost (finding a tutor you like often forces you to cycle through a few that you don’t)" (HN).
- "Human tutors help, but they can be costly, hard to schedule" (YCL, as summarised).
- No time or place is named. **[author]**:
  - Circumstance "they want to practise speaking the language", occasion "practice session", window {7, DAYS}, Frequency 3 to 7 days out of 7, Prevalence "Most" (p_60_80).
  - These are the smallest choice for a daily-habit product, which the founders' "instantly speak and immerse yourself" (HN) implies.

**4. Which people (comparable group).**
- Intermediate and advanced learners (item 1). YCL addresses people "serious about improving their foreign language skills" (as summarised).
- **[author]** The Importance rivals are the difficulties the thread itself names:
  - vocabulary: the founders' "word bank and SRS flashcards" (HN)
  - understanding natives at speed: HN/44395109's "understanding accents/pronunciations quickly enough"
  - grammar: HN/44395682's "embarrassing holes"
  - finding time: HN/44395109's 2.5 hours a weekday
- The own item, "Finding someone to speak with when it suits", is the founders' scheduling pain in a learner's words.

**5. Who pays.**
- The learner, by subscription: "Pricing: 20 min free trial, $20–29/month" (HN).
- **[author]** Buyer and payer is "Nobody else" only. The founders name no other role. One respondent (Simon Achebe) shows the spouse the thread raises: "I would have a hard time justifying an additional subscription to my wife!" (HN/44389205).

**6. Mechanism.**
- "a custom voice AI pipeline combining STT (speech-to-text), TTS (text-to-speech), LLMs, long term memory, interruptions, turn-taking" (HN).
- "a word bank and SRS flashcards for new words learned in the AI voice chats" (HN).
- "custom curriculums for each student based on goals, interests, and preferences" (HN).
- "works on web, iOS, Android" (HN).
- The `not_assumed` item "the tutor catches pronunciation mistakes" comes from the founder's own answer: "Yes we do have this issue" (HN/44389905).
- Compatibility conditions **[author]**:
  - The tested one, "They could already hold a simple conversation", is the founders' not-for-beginners line, turned into a condition.
  - "speak aloud" draws on HN/44396663, and "steady connection" on HN/44390909 ("it's all server side", HN/44390965).
- Adoption friction **[author]**:
  - The tested effort, "Talk out loud to an AI tutor", is the product's one act.
  - The intro conversation comes from "There is a structured curriculum that gets generated after the intro lesson" (HN/44389578).
- Commitment step **[author]**: "pay for one month after the trial", the first paid act after "20 min free trial" (HN).

**7. Price.**
- "$20–29/month (depending on duration and specific geography)" (HN). The founder's price is $20 to $29 a month.
- Tutor cost: "$20/hour on italki on average" (YCL, as summarised; cited there from Glassdoor).
- **[author]** The cost estimate, $80 to $160 a month, is that hourly rate times one to two lessons a week (4 to 8 lessons a month). It is the smallest reading of "you pay by the hour" (HN).
- Ability to pay is derived by code: 13% to 36%, small_share.

**8. Occasions (real accounts).**
- 271 comments, many of them first-person learners. Each respondent below is traced to one.
- The thread also holds the price objection: "I found the pricing and it’s a tough sell! ChatGPT is cheaper." (HN/44389205).
- It holds the trust objection: "I think I would pay for this if I wasn't worried about learning mispronunciations or errors" (HN/44390451).

## Respondents

- Caleb Nguyen: HN/44388565 (Vietnamese; "I pay $160/mo for Vietnamese tutoring ($20 per class) … I don't have to schedule my classes"). The rescheduling is **[author]**.
- Rosa Delgado-Hart: HN/44391306 ("I currently pay $99 a month to learn Spanish from a live tutor 30 mins a day").
- Patrick Sorensen: HN/44395109 (Thai; "30 minutes every weekday doing flashcards, 45 minutes with a tutor … To save $2,700 a year") and HN/44389181.
- Yuki Brennan: HN/44396663 ("I think I'm around A2 in Japanese … I don't mind texting … but talking just makes me feel very anxious") and HN/44390432 (skipping the textbook's speaking exercises).
- Jin-ho Park: HN/44388971 ("second-gen Korean-American; my korean is weak but conversational"). The call with an aunt is **[author]**.
- Astrid Mallory: HN/44388547 and HN/44388629 (Swedish: "I can have unstructured conversations … in real life here in Sweden", wants "a guided learning experience").
- Derek Holloway: HN/44388976 (ChatGPT voice mode, "pick a random blurb in the news", "an hour long foreign language practice in Spanish while walking my husky"). His $20 a month for ChatGPT is **[author]**.
- Nikos Ferrante: HN/44388531 (Greek "as a beginner … I still got lost 5 minutes in … a long sentence in Greek about how how it is nice to hike in mountains"). He is outside the segment on purpose: beginners reached the real app.
- Laura Pennington (gate No): HN/44388467 ("lost any semblance of proficiency -- mainly because I never have a real occasion to use anything other than English").
- Mateo Lindgren: HN/44388794 ("I used italki extensively and found having a live Columbian tutor invaluable and very affordable … It would genuinely make me sad if those excellent tutors start losing work"). Medellín and $15 are **[author]**.
- Farida Haque: HN/44388539 ("Assimil courses and done lots of comprehensible input … language production is typically the weak point … plenty of lessons on iTalki"). Moving her to French is **[author]**.
- Simon Achebe: HN/44389205 ("Frantastic is absurdly expensive and it made me switch to italki … justifying an additional subscription to my wife").
- Gabriel Stein: HN/44395682 ("living in Buenos Aires for over 18 years … my pronunciations and accent is quite good … a bunch of embarrassing holes").
- Lucía Moreno: HN/44396239 (Chinese "somewhere between HSK 2 and 3 … When I babble … it cuts me off in the first eh"; a native Spanish speaker). The exchange partner is **[author]**.
- Imani Brooks: HN/44396656 ("~Japanese N4, A2 … living outside of Japan, struggle to find good opportunities to output"). Ohio is **[author]**.
- Arjun Kapoor: HN/44390909 ("I do all my language learning on the commuter trains w/o a good connection") and HN/44390855 (Urdu). Urdu as his family's language is **[author]**.
- Tobias Wren (chip): HN/44389852 ("As an intermediate German speaker"). The refusal to say more is an author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story is needed so the reading counts one GUESSED person.
- Megan Ashford: HN/44390650 (Russian; "the AI won't spot areas where you e.g. fudge a case ending or the stress on a word").
- Hassan El-Amin (gate No): author's invention, filling a gap. No commenter describes a week without wanting to practise, and a realistic gate needs one in-segment No beside the out-of-practice Laura Pennington.
- Priya Natarajan: HN/44392491 ("I don't think I can trust TTS for language learning. I could be internalizing wrong pronunciation") and HN/44390451 ("I would pay for this if I wasn't worried about learning mispronunciations").

No respondent carries a commenter's handle or a real person's name.

## Open

- **Relative advantage code.** None of the registry's five advantage codes means "available any time". I used `less_help_needed` with the founder's label "Speaking practice any time, no tutor to book", because it drops the tutor. `shorter_time` was the other candidate.
- **YC launch wording.** The WebFetch summaries of YCL and YCC were paraphrases, not full text. The two YCL phrases above marked "as summarised" may differ slightly from the page. Every HN quote is verbatim from the thread's API text.
- **Cost estimate.** The $80 to $160 a month is my arithmetic on "$20/hour on italki on average", not a founder statement. Several respondents spend nothing, because the problem's cost to them is the missing practice, not money. So Existing sacrifice is likely to read below the founder's estimate.
- **Market.** US is assumed. Issen prices "depending on duration and specific geography", and nothing public names a US focus.
- **Not checked against the engine.** The file passes keel-e2e-eval's `instructions/corpus.py` loader (bound to the registry) and every rule of `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` but S/V. Those need the `expected` block, which a back-test omits by design.

screens.why_b5: The 7 stays visible, 'among these 7' is honest and 'Holding up' is modest, but the page never says that 7 is a small group, and 'People disagree' slightly softens a Current solution result that is 2 short of the bar.
screens.instead: Not settled yet, among only 7 people: most want more speaking practice and rank it high, but only 3 of 7 say today's way falls short (bar 5), so before building on it, find out what the other 4 are satisfied with.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up above your band' sits directly above the number that decides it, 7 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7.
screens.why_b2: The strip counts the people who said yes, runs 0 to 7 with all 7 cells for me, and marks the bar at 5, so all three are plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: The practise-speaking wording is mine, but 'Prevalence' is Keel's label, this belief isn't among the two I'm shown as checked, and my 'most' has become '6 to 7 in 10'.
screens.why_b4: It says the want is common among these 7 and points to the next two cards, but not what that means for Issen: wanting to practise is only the entry condition, so it doesn't yet justify the product.
screens.why_b5: The claim stays with 'among these 7', n is visible, and the low n is stated as 'a small group: a lean, not a call', so 7 of 7 is not oversold.
screens.instead: All 7 wanted to practise speaking this week, so the want is there among these few, but that alone doesn't show they'd pay for Issen; how often they want it and how much it matters decide that.

screens.why_b1: "People disagree" sits directly above the deciding numbers, 4 of 7 in my band against a bar of 5, 1 short, so I know my belief did not clear the bar and why.
screens.why_b2: Days out of 7, the 7 people and the median are plain, but the median of 3 sits inside my band while the 5-of-7 bar counts people on a chart whose axis counts days, so I need a second look to see why it fell short.
screens.why_b3: Frequency, 3 to 7 days out of 7 and wanting to practise speaking are my own belief and words, with only the minor oddity of "at or beyond" for a band that ends at 7.
screens.why_b4: The So line restates the count and defers with "Whether it matters is the next card", so it never says what a 3-day floor means for a daily-practice product or what I should do about it.
screens.why_b5: All 7 answers stay visible, the screen says "a small group: a lean, not a call", and the 4-to-3 split is called a disagreement rather than a finding about all learners.
screens.instead: 4 of 7 want to practise on 3 or more days, 1 short of your bar of 5, and the other 3 want to on fewer than 3, so with only 7 people don't build around a daily habit yet: ask more learners and see on the next card whether speaking practice matters enough to them.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "5 of 7 put it in their two · bar 5 of 7 · at the bar", so I know my belief held, only just, and which number decides it.
screens.why_b2: The caption and the bar are clear and speaking practice visibly leads, but the bars count 14 picks while my bar counts 7 people, and the strip's "for 5, against 9" takes a second look because only 2 people count against me.
screens.why_b3: The title is Importance and the belief line is word for word the one I checked, with "Too little speaking practice" marked as the problem I named.
screens.why_b4: The So line tells me how to read the number (top two, not first) but not what it means for Issen, so I have to work out the next step myself from the two quotes about anxiety and about grammar and words.
screens.why_b5: It keeps n visible, says "among these 7" and "a small group: a lean, not a call", and warns that top two does not mean first, so nothing claims more than the data carries.
screens.instead: Say: 5 of 7 is exactly at the bar, so one person the other way and it would not hold; speaking practice is a real pain for these 7, but the two who passed over it wanted words and grammar first, so test the word bank and flashcards alongside the voice tutor. And draw the strip by people, 5 for and 2 against, not 5 and 9.

screens.why_b1: 3 of 7 against a bar of 5, 2 short, is clear and sits right beside the verdict, but 'People disagree' never tells me plainly that my belief did not reach its bar.
screens.why_b2: I can see the five answers, the 7 people and the 3-for, 4-against split at once, but it takes a second look to separate 'your line' between the answers from 'your bar' of 5 of 7.
screens.why_b3: The title and belief line match what I checked on the way in, including my clumsy 'booking a tutor, or otherwise practising speaking alone' wording, and the line is the same 'Spoke enough, after planning around a tutor'.
screens.why_b4: It tells me the belief fell short and sends me to Insights to see what keeps today's way working, but it doesn't say what this means for Issen, such as whether tutor-bookers are a weak opening or whether to aim at those who can't find anyone to speak with.
screens.why_b5: It rightly says 7 is 'a lean, not a call', but 'after planning around a tutor and are content' overstates: Caleb has moved class twice this month, Rosa calls it pricey, and Derek uses a chatbot with no tutor at all.
screens.instead: Not held: 3 of 7 fell short against a bar of 5, a lean from 7 people; of the 3 who spoke enough, two pay a tutor and put up with cost or rescheduling and one already gets by on a cheap chatbot, so test whether Issen beats those before building on tutor frustration.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on its verdict with the deciding number beside it: People disagree with 3 of 7 against a bar of 5, 2 short, and Holding up with 5 of 7 at the bar.
screens.why_b3: The names Current solution and Importance and both belief lines are the ones I checked on the way in, clumsy 'streak-rewarding programs' wording included.
screens.why_b4: The screen gives quotes and counts but never says what this means for Issen, such as whether to sharpen against ChatGPT voice mode or tutors, or to narrow the segment, so the next step is left entirely to me.
screens.why_b5: The counts stay visible and Astrid's absence is named, but 'Importance held, 5 of 7' is stated flatly when one person would flip it, and nothing says that 7 people is a small group.
screens.why_b6: The quotes add what I did not type: a cheap chatbot voice mode already 'works fine', tutor rescheduling annoys without breaking the habit, anxiety keeps one learner from speaking at all, and someone who speaks daily is stuck on grammar and words instead.
screens.instead: Today's way mostly works for these people: a chatbot voice mode is cheap and a booked tutor keeps them speaking despite the rescheduling, so test Issen against those two, and treat Importance as thin because 5 of 7 sits at the bar and one person would flip it.

screens.why1: As the first screen of a study about learning a language, it makes sense to check straight away whether I'm a beginner or already on my way.
screens.why2: I can answer it, but the present-tense 'starting from zero' reads a bit oddly for someone already taking classes, and it takes a second to see it means 'are you a total beginner'.
screens.why3: I know exactly where I stand with my Vietnamese after paying for regular tutoring, so this is easy to answer from my own life.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it cleanly, and a screener like this needs no escape, because I either am a total beginner or I'm not.
screens.why5: It keeps the idea of not starting from zero, and nothing about a product, a company or a label like 'intermediate learner' reaches me.
screens.why6: It is one short question with two options, easy to hear once and answer, though 'I'll read 2 options' is a little stiff before a plain yes or no.
screens.instead: Are you a complete beginner in the language you're learning? Yes or no.

screens.why1: After checking I'm not a beginner, it makes sense to ask whether I wanted to practise speaking this past week, since that's what the study seems to be about.
screens.why2: I understand it the first time, and 'practise speaking the language' is how I'd describe my $20 tutoring classes and speaking practice.
screens.why3: I know whether I wanted to practise Vietnamese in the last week, so I can answer straight from my own life.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but 'I can't recall one particular conversation' doesn't fit a question about wanting to practise, and there are two escape chips on a yes-or-no question where 'I'd rather not say' adds nothing.
screens.why5: Nothing here hints at a product or company, and it reads as a plain question about wanting to practise speaking.
screens.why6: Said aloud, it's one short question ending in 'Yes or no', so I can answer after hearing it once.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you want to practise speaking the language? Yes / No (no escape chips)

screens.why1: I just said yes to wanting to practise in the last week, so asking how many days follows naturally.
screens.why2: The words are easy, but 'wanted to practise' on a given day is a little fuzzy for me, because I take classes and the want is more or less always there, so I would pause over what counts.
screens.why3: I know my class days and when I actually spoke, but how many days I merely wanted to practise is something I never track, so I would be partly guessing.
screens.why4: One to seven covers every answer after my yes on the last screen, the numbers cannot overlap, and 'I can't recall' fits as the escape.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product or company reaches me, and it just asks about wanting to practise speaking.
screens.why6: It is one short question with a simple 'say a number from 1 to 7' and one escape, so I could hear it once and answer.

screens.why1: After asking how often I wanted to practise speaking, it makes sense to ask what I'd most like made easier in my week of learning Vietnamese.
screens.why2: I understand it on first reading, and words like grammar, native speakers and speaking practice are how learners already talk.
screens.why3: I can answer from my last week of tutoring classes and study without guessing.
screens.why4: "Too little speaking practice" names a problem while the others name a task, so it doesn't fit "made easier", and arranging or paying for speaking time with a tutor has no clear option, though "None of these" fits as the escape.
screens.why5: It stays on speaking and learning a language, with no sign of a product, a company plan or founder terms, and speaking practice sits among ordinary learner troubles.
screens.why6: It's short and five short options are easy to hold, but "made easier" followed by "too little speaking practice" sounds wrong when heard and makes me stop for a moment.
screens.instead: Think of your last week of learning the language. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Remembering new words; understanding native speakers at full speed; getting enough speaking practice; finding time to study at all; or getting the grammar right. Or say none of these.

screens.why1: After being asked what I wanted to practise and what I'd most like easier, it makes sense to ask how my actual speaking practice went.
screens.why2: "Booking a tutor, or otherwise practising speaking alone with streak-rewarding programs" is a tangle that bundles two different things, "streak-rewarding programs" isn't how I'd say Duolingo-type apps, and "your last conversation" clashes with practising alone.
screens.why3: I can say how my tutoring went, but "last conversation" is unclear (my last class, or any chat in Vietnamese?), and if I just did a class I have to guess how apps fit in.
screens.why4: The range covers my life, but "Spoke a little; costly or hard to book" joins two causes, and a tutor I can afford who is still a scheduling hassle sits between the first three options.
screens.why5: No product leaks, but "streak-rewarding programs" reads like someone's written-up framing of the market rather than anything a learner says, and it slants the question against apps.
screens.why6: Heard once, the stem's "booking a tutor, or otherwise practising speaking alone with streak-rewarding programs" is two ideas in one breath that I couldn't hold, and the options with their causes tacked on are a lot to keep after it.
screens.instead: Think of the last time you wanted to practise speaking. How did it go? Spoke as much as I wanted; spoke, after working around a tutor's schedule; spoke a little, it was too costly or hard to book; only practised alone, with an app; or didn't get to speak at all. Or say you can't recall.

screens.why1: Asking what keeps it working is an obvious follow-up to having just said how booking a tutor or practising went for me.
screens.why2: I can answer it, but I'd have to read 'booking a tutor, or otherwise practising speaking alone with streak-rewarding programs' twice, and I'd never say 'streak-rewarding programs' when I mean apps like Duolingo.
screens.why3: I can say what keeps my weekly tutor classes going, but the question lumps them with streak apps I may not use, and it doesn't fit that rescheduling is the part that doesn't work for me.
screens.why4: It's a box to type in, with no options or escape to judge.
screens.why5: 'Streak-rewarding programs' sounds like someone's market description rather than anything a learner says, and it hints at how the people behind the study categorise what I do.
screens.why6: It's two short sentences with a clear ask at the end, but the long clause is a mouthful heard once, and by the time it reaches 'streak-rewarding programs' I've half lost what I supposedly said.
screens.instead: You said the way you practise speaking works for you, like booking a tutor or using an app. What keeps it working?
